paragraphs: In the Gettysburg Address, Abraham Lincoln develops two central ideas: that the Civil War is the ultimate test of whether a nation founded on human equality can survive, and that the living must honor the fallen by fighting to preserve that democracy. Lincoln begins in the past by reminding his audience of the nation's founding, stating that our ancestors created a country "conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal." He then shifts to the present conflict, explaining that the Civil War is "testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure." Finally, Lincoln looks to the future and connects these ideas by arguing that the best way to consecrate the battlefield is for citizens to dedicate themselves to the "unfinished work" left behind. He urges the audience to ensure that "these dead shall not have died in vain" so that "government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth." These ideas were especially critical in 1863 because the Union was suffering heavy casualties and facing war weariness, so Lincoln needed to give people a powerful moral purpose to keep fighting and prove that self-government could truly endure.
